title: Reading Workshop? Goals, Outcomes, and Objectives
author: Dr. Andy Johnson
summary: Andy Johnson opens a two-part examination of reading workshop, which the National Council on Teacher Quality lists among practices 'contrary to the science of reading'. Rather than defending or attacking the model, he asks what research actually supports that verdict and argues that instructional approaches should be judged against the goals, outcomes and objectives a school holds. He defines each term: a goal is the big picture, outcomes are long-term intentions, and objectives are the short-term, observable steps toward an outcome. Using two contrasting sets of literacy outcomes, he shows that workshop suits aims such as reading for pleasure and stamina, while commercial structured programs suit narrower, test-oriented aims, and notes that publishers' goals differ from schools' goals. He ends by deriving observable objectives for the outcome of motivation to read, among them choice, access, daily time, goal-setting and conversation about books.
points: Reading approaches should be evaluated against explicit goals, outcomes and objectives, not labelled good or bad in the abstract.
Goals are the big picture, outcomes are long-term intentions, and objectives are short-term steps that are observable and measurable.
Reading workshop is a strong fit for outcomes like voluntary reading, stamina, and applying literacy to real-world contexts.
Commercial reading programs have their own goals, so their claims should be read alongside the publisher's incentive to maximize profit.
Motivation to read can be built through measurable conditions: choice, access, daily reading time, goal-setting and book conversation.
quotes: Reading workshop is on the list of practices deemed “contrary to the science of reading” by the National Council on Teacher Quality (Ellis, et at., 2026) (see Figure 7.1). The question is, why? Why is reading workshop a bad thing?
There is no “best way” to teach reading. However, there are some approaches that may be better suited for achieving desired goals and outcomes than others.
A goal is what you hope to accomplish. It’s the big picture. We get so busy looking at the little parts that sometimes we forget that it’s the big picture that’s most important.
Outcomes are broad intentions or things you hope to bring about as a result of something, in this case, reading instruction. These are your long-term intentions.
When you look at brochures and websites for commercial reading products, consider that Big Publishing has different goals and outcomes than schools do.
Objectives are more specific than outcomes and are short term. Objective are the steps needed to achieve a desired outcome. Also, objectives are measurable or observable.
Good objectives are created by first considering the desired outcome then identifying the conditions necessary to achieve it.
In the hands of a skilled teacher, you can create the conditions that enable all students to develop their full literacy potential.
